ABSTRACT Background The kynurenine pathway (KP) plays a pivotal role in many diseases that involve distinct pathological mechanisms. Objectives Since KP metabolites are potential disease biomarkers, it is crucial to investigate their fluctuations under physiological conditions. As the KP is stress‐responsive, this study examines how peripheral KP metabolites change with core temperature increases induced by two different modalities. Methods In this randomized cross‐over study, 11 young healthy males were subjected to (a) exogenous heating via hot water immersion (44°C, EXO), and (b) exertional heating via exercise (EXE), until rectal temperature ( T rec ) reached 39°C, followed by a recovery phase. Blood samples were collected at baseline and at every 0.5°C T rec increment during both the heating and recovery phases. Plasma levels of KP metabolites, stress, and metabolic markers were measured. Correlation analyses between kynurenine pathway metabolites and stress markers were computed over the course of the trials. Results EXE and EXO trials induced the KP, but to different extents. Most plasma KP metabolite concentrations (kynurenic acid, picolinic acid, 3‐hydrokynurenine, quinolinic acid) increased. Stress markers were elevated in both trials. Changes in KP metabolites, stress, and metabolic markers were not persistent, and returned to baseline following recovery. Funding: This work was supported by grants from the Vetenskapsrådet (2024‐02812), the Hjärnfonden (FO2022‐0140), Åhlén‐stiftelsen and the Initiative for Excellence in Universities Science and Sport Lithuania (No. S‐A‐UEI‐23‐2). 1 Introduction The kynurenine pathway (KP) is the primary route of tryptophan (TRP) degradation, generating physiologically active metabolites with diverse functions. While KP in the brain primarily originates from astrocytes, its peripheral activity is mainly localized in the liver and skeletal muscles. Metabolites produced along this pathway are increasingly recognized for their roles in neurological and psychiatric disorders, as well as playing a role in immune responses, cardiovascular function, and energy metabolism [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ]. Metabolites such as kynurenine (KYN), kynurenic acid (KYNA), quinolinic acid (QUIN), and picolinic acid (PIC) have been proposed as biomarkers for tracking disease severity and progression across various conditions [ 5 , 6 ]. Understanding the regulation of this pathway in healthy individuals, both at rest and under physiological stress, is essential for assessing its dysfunction in disease states. Physiological stressors such as exercise and caloric restriction have been shown to induce the KP, with cortisol identified as a trigger in this regard [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ]. Heat exposure, a universal physiological stressor, triggers thermoregulatory mechanisms and activates both neuronal and physiological processes [ 11 ]. Heat stress can be induced through exertional (EXE) means, such as exercise, which raises body temperature through muscle contraction and increased metabolic rates [ 12 ], or through exogenous (EXO) methods like hot‐water immersion [ 13 ]. Hot‐water immersion, a passive technique, is frequently used in both research and clinical settings to raise core body temperature without mechanical strain [ 12 , 13 , 14 ]. Even slight increases in core temperature are thought to provoke a modest, but rapid, inflammatory response [ 15 , 16 ]. In addition to passive heating, exercise also produces stress‐induced immune activation, but with a more pronounced response [ 17 , 18 ]. In parallel, ample evidence indicates the activation of the kynurenine pathway by exercise or infection [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ]. From a functional perspective, if an increase in body temperature alone is a sufficient component to activate the KP, this could offer therapeutic potential for managing diseases involving dysregulation of the KP. It is well‐established that heat stress involves activation of both the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) and the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis. The SNS provides rapid adaptation to stressors through the release of catecholamines such as noradrenaline and adrenaline [ 24 ]. This response increases heart rate and redistributes blood flow to promote sweating and the regulation of body temperature. In contrast, the HPA axis triggers slower mechanisms involving cortisol production [ 25 ]. These responses are critical as both catecholamines and cortisol profoundly influence metabolism and immune functions, thereby impacting KP, especially under physiological stress [ 7 , 9 , 10 , 26 ]. While the majority of research on KP has been focused on its role in pathophysiological states [ 2 , 3 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 ], relatively few studies have examined its regulation in healthy individuals, and among these, the majority have examined how exercise influences KP metabolites [ 9 , 10 , 31 , 32 ]. This study is the first to examine the effects of core temperature elevation on KP metabolites in healthy males. More specifically, the aim is to investigate the effects of two distinct heat stress modalities on KP metabolites. Additionally, we aim to examine whether well‐established stress markers would indirectly reflect the KP kinetics observed during the different heat stress modalities. To capture any delayed effects that might emerge post‐heating, samples were also collected during the recovery phase. We hypothesize that both passive heating and a rise in body temperature due to exercise will initiate a stress response, affecting the concentration of KP metabolites. We expect the EXE trial to produce more pronounced effects due to the additional cardiovascular, mechanical, and metabolic demands associated with exercise. Specifically, EXE uniquely activates skeletal muscle, a major source of peripheral KYNA, which should lead to higher plasma KYNA levels [ 8 , 32 ] than EXO. Additionally, we hypothesize that other biomarkers, such as catecholamines, will be particularly affected in the EXE trial and may parallel changes in KP metabolites, while prolactin levels are expected to be more responsive in the EXO trial due to its sensitivity to skin temperature [ 33 ].

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Heat exposure and exercise stress, specifically through exertional heating (cycling exercise at 60% VO2max in 30°C) and exogenous heating (hot water immersion at 44°C), designed to elevate core rectal temperature (Trec) to 39°C.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: The kynurenine pathway (KP) is stress-responsive, and an elevation in body temperature due to heat exposure or exercise increases peripheral concentrations of several KP metabolites, indicating the adaptability of KP enzymes to physiological stressors. Heat stress and exercise activate both the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) and the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis. SNS activation leads to rapid release of catecholamines (noradrenaline, adrenaline), resulting in pronounced and rapid elevation of these markers, which positively associate with the KYN/TRP ratio. The HPA axis triggers slower mechanisms involving cortisol production, which shows a gradual rise, peaking in the recovery phase. These hormones profoundly influence metabolism and immune functions, impacting the KP. The additional exercise stress in the EXE trial, particularly muscle strain from cycling, induces greater sympathetic vasomotor activity and adrenaline release, leading to stronger KP activation. Exercise also stimulates PGC-1α expression in skeletal muscle, increasing KAT enzyme expression (contributing to elevated peripheral KYNA) and inducing ACMSD expression (responsible for PIC production). Elevated PIC is linked to increased acetyl-CoA synthesis, feeding into the tricarboxylic acid cycle. NAD+ generation via the KP influences nicotinamide (NAM) levels, with acute exercise increasing NAD+ metabolic enzyme expression. Excess KYNA, potentially via aryl hydrocarbon receptor stimulation, might further modulate NAD+ metabolism and NAM availability. Correlation analyses revealed general similarities in noradrenaline and adrenaline patterns with KP metabolites across trials, but cortisol correlations differed, notably a positive correlation between KYNA and cortisol at 39°C during the EXO trial.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Both Exertional (EXE) and Exogenous (EXO) heating trials induced the kynurenine pathway (KP) and achieved a comparable increase in rectal temperature (Trec) to 39°C within similar timeframes, without inducing extreme heat stress. However, the extent and specific biomarker responses differed. The EXE trial consistently induced a greater increase in stress markers (catecholamines, cortisol) and showed more widespread significant increases across KP metabolites (e.g., KYN, QUIN, PIC). The increase in KYNA was more evident in EXE (from 52.9 nM to 83.7 nM) compared to EXO (from 52.6 to 65.7 nM) during recovery. PSI showed a greater increase upon EXE (p < 0.0001). Conversely, Prolactin showed the greatest increase upon EXO (p < 0.01). PIC and NAM values were significantly different between post-intervention trials (p < 0.05 and p < 0.01 respectively). Specific effects of EXO on KYNA, QUIN, and NAM were dependent on water temperature.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The stronger activation of the KP and stress markers observed in the Exertional (EXE) trial, leading to more pronounced effects on specific KP metabolites like KYNA, 3-HK, and PIC, is attributed to the additional exercise stress and muscle strain associated with cycling, not solely the heat exposure. EXE uniquely activates skeletal muscle, a major source of peripheral KYNA, hypothesized to result in higher plasma KYNA levels. Conversely, prolactin levels were more responsive in the Exogenous (EXO) trial, likely due to its sensitivity to skin temperature. 3-HK and PIC levels were primarily affected only in the EXE trial, indicating specificity to this intervention type. The QUIN/KYNA ratio gradually declined in EXE but remained largely unchanged in EXO. While noradrenaline and adrenaline generally showed similar correlation patterns with KP metabolites across trials, cortisol correlations differed, with a specific positive correlation between KYNA and cortisol identified at 39°C during the EXO trial. The effects observed in the EXO trial were dependent on water temperature, suggesting specificity to thermal stress rather than water immersion alone.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: The study directly involved 11 healthy young males, aged 18 to 36 years, who were physically active (exercising 2-3 times per week). Participants were rigorously screened to exclude individuals with health conditions such as smoking, medication use, BMI > 30 kg/m2, asthma, neurological conditions, cardiovascular disease, or any condition adversely affected by core temperature elevation, and no prior temperature manipulation programs. Broader implications extend to patients with depression, type 2 diabetes, and individuals suffering from neurological, psychiatric, cardiovascular disorders, cancer, infectious diseases, schizophrenia, and bipolar disorder.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: This study enhances the understanding of how the kynurenine pathway (KP) is regulated in healthy individuals under physiological stress, which is crucial for assessing its dysfunction in various disease states. The characterization of physiological and metabolic responses to heat stress, including changes in stress markers, heart rate, and KP metabolites, provides insights into human health. KP metabolites are implicated in neurological, psychiatric, and cardiovascular disorders, as well as cancer, due to their influence on glutamatergic and dopaminergic signaling. The findings suggest that if an increase in body temperature alone can activate the KP, it holds potential for therapeutic strategies in managing diseases involving KP dysregulation. Furthermore, exercise is highlighted for its broad benefits in both health and disease, including symptom improvements for conditions like depression.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: The study indicates diagnostic utility for KP metabolites as potential disease biomarkers, particularly for monitoring physiological strain and metabolic changes during heat stress. While the controlled induction of temporary core temperature elevation in healthy individuals, coupled with strict exclusion criteria, aims to minimize adverse effects, the heat stress exposure itself elicits stress responses, implying an inherent adverse risk. Conversely, the findings also suggest a protective benefit from exercise for overall health and disease management.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The reliability of the measurements was generally high: rectal temperature probes had an accuracy of ±0.01°C (considered gold standard); UPLC-MS/MS for TRP and KP metabolites (KYN, KYNA, 3-HK, PIC, QUIN, NAM) showed intra-assay coefficient of variation (CV) less than 9%. Plasma adrenaline and noradrenaline had intra-assay CVs of 2.01% and 5.91% respectively, with inter-assay CVs of 2.02% and 7.12%. Serum prolactin had intra-assay and inter-assay CVs of 4.59% and 4.48%, respectively. Salivary free cortisol measurements showed an intra-assay CV of 2.94% and an inter-assay CV of 8.79%. The study's cross-over design enhanced the robustness of the results, despite a small sample size. However, a limitation was the exclusive focus on young male participants, which restricts generalizability as age and sex are known to influence heat tolerance. It was also noted that slight, unavoidable differences in room temperature occurred between trials. The overall findings suggest that observed changes in KP metabolites, stress, and metabolic markers were transient, returning to baseline following recovery, indicating the adaptability of KP enzymes to physiological stressors rather than persistent alteration.
